newsitem.title: CHINA: China to charge dissident for anti-government plot.
newsitem.headline: China to charge dissident for anti-government plot.

text.p: Chinese dissident and former student leader Wang Dan faces a second jail term after prosecutors charged him recently with subversion, Chinese sources said on Monday.
A court in Beijing was expected to deliver a verdict on Wang's case this week, said one source, who declined to be identified.
Wang, 26, faces up to seven years in jail on charges of counter-revolutionary incitement, or subversion, the source said.
His family declined to comment on Wang's whereabouts and said they had no news of their son.

Wang disappeared into a security limbo after he was detained in May 1995, in the run-up to the sixth anniversary of the June 1989 military crackdown that crushed student-led protests for A former student of Beijing University, he served four years in jail for counter-revolutionary activities for his role as a leader of the 1989 demonstrations.
He had been expected to face charges because the court that convicted veteran democracy activist Wei Jingsheng last December of plotting to overthrow the government implicated Wang in its verdict.

That verdict said Wei, who was jailed for 14 years, had links with people "convicted of counter-revolutionary crimes, including Wang Dan." It also referred to a tape-recorded conversation between Wang and Wei, but gave no details.

Wei, nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1995 and 1996 and who served 14-1/2 years of a 15-year sentence for counter-revolution before his release on parole in September 1993, is regarded as the father of China's tiny, struggling democracy movement.
Wang had been active since his release from jail, defying persistent police surveillance and harassment.

Police raided his home in May, 1995, just days after he joined 44 people in signing a daring appeal to Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin demanding the release of all those still in prison for their part in the 1989 demonstrations centred in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Wang was last seen in an unusual police video issued two months after his detention to counter reports he was on a hunger strike -- a protest he had pledged to carry out if arrested.

That three-minute narrated videotape, made in a detention centre under the Beijing Reform through Labour Department, said Wang was legally detained on May 21 for "disturbing the social order" and said he refused meals for just two days.
Wang was one of a very few Chinese dissidents who are not serving jail terms or re-education through labour penalties.
A court in central Henan province last month sentenced student leader-turned-dissident Guo Haifeng to seven years in prison for hooliganism.
Police had initially accused Guo of fraud but the prosecutor did not file charges against him, a human rights group said.

A Hong Kong newspaper reported in August that Guo was detained and was suspected of helping Liu Gang, another leader of the 1989 student demonstrations that were crushed by the military, flee to the United States in April.
Guo, a former student of Beijing University, was sentenced in 1991 to four years in prison for counter-revolutionary sabotage.
